slides.body: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery.
Today you follow one push through its seven steps and see where it can be refused, by whom, and with which words.
The server in the demos is a bare repository on disk, which means it has no working tree, only the Git data.
Here's what you'll walk away with.

slides.body: Do Exercise 7.3, Level 1, "publish a branch, then delete it on the server", and Exercise 7.8, Level 3, "a push that the other side refuses", both in exercises/m06-m10-integration.md.
Today you read a push as a request with two gatekeepers, and you can tell from one word which of them said no.

beats.text: Two engineers sit next to each other. Both have one local commit on main. Both push. One gets "fetch first". The other gets "non-fast-forward". They are in the same situation: a colleague pushed before them.
beats.tele: Two engineers sit next to each other. Both have one local commit on `main`. Both push. One gets "fetch first". The other gets "non-fast-forward". They are in the same situation: a colleague pushed before them.

beats.text: Why two messages for one cause? And here is the question that tells you whether someone understands push: in both cases, who said no? Their own Git, or the server? The answer is on the screen, in one word, and most people have never read it.

beats.text: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery. Pull up a chair. Fetch reads another repository. Push writes to one. That makes push the first command in this module that can change something you do not own, and so it's the first where another party gets a vote.

beats.text: Today you follow one push through its seven steps and see where it can be refused, by whom, and with which words. Then you push the things that are not branches of the ordinary kind: deletions, tags, several refs at once. You look at pushes that fail before any comparison is made. You look at the rules a plain Git server can enforce. And you close with section 12.9: why Git refuses a push into a branch that somebody has checked out.

beats.text: A push runs in a fixed order, and you will have the order on screen as today's diagram. In short: your Git reads the server's refs. Your Git applies client rules to each ref you want to update. If they fail, nothing is sent. If they pass, your Git sends a line per ref, "old, new, ref name", plus a packfile, one file that holds the objects.

If they pass, your Git sends a line per ref, "old, new, ref name", plus a packfile, one file that holds the objects.

beats.text: The server puts the objects into a quarantine directory, checks that the ref is still at the old value, applies its receive.deny* settings and runs its hooks, which are scripts Git runs at a defined point. If all of that passes, the refs are updated. Last, your Git moves your remote-tracking ref.

beats.text: The client rules are in the manual's "push rules": an existing branch may only be fast-forwarded, which means moved to a descendant of the commit it has now. An existing tag may not be updated at all. And creations and deletions are allowed unless configuration or hooks forbid them. On screen is today's case, as your clone sees it: one commit of yours on top of 510ee94, where origin/main still sits. Whether pushing it is a fast-forward depends on where the server's main really is.

beats.text: Your branch, your index and your working tree: unchanged. A push does not alter your work. It alters theirs.

beats.text: And section 12.9 in two sentences. A push moves refs. It checks nothing out. So if the pushed ref is the branch that the receiving repository has checked out, that repository's HEAD would name a commit that its index and working tree do not match, and its next git status would present the pushed changes as local edits that undo them. Git refuses by default.
